title: Key-value stores and DynamoDB basics
goal: By the end, you can say what a key-value store answers and where it stops, store and read payments in DynamoDB from a Kotlin class, make a payment that arrives twice land once with a conditional write, and read an account's newest payments with one Query.
opening:
Picture the café at lunchtime. You tap your card, and the card reader sends the payment to the payments company's program. The program stores it in DynamoDB and answers, but the answer is slow, and the reader gives up waiting. So it sends the exact same payment again. The first one had arrived. Only its answer was late.

It's easy to assume the database will notice the repeat. In JSONB, upserts and MERGE, PostgreSQL did, because a unique index refused the second copy. A store built around keys plays by its own rules, and what happens depends on what the key is made of.

Model the access patterns first turned the app's questions into two-part keys. In this lesson, we'll build the simplest store a key can serve, then store payments in DynamoDB on your laptop from a Kotlin class. We'll make that repeated payment land once, and read an account's newest payments with one request. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The program stores a payment in DynamoDB with one write call, `PutItem`. The answer is slow, the card reader gives up, and the exact same `PutItem` is sent again. The first one had in fact succeeded. What is in the table now?
options: Two items, one for each PutItem
One item: the second PutItem replaced the first, without an error
One item, and the second PutItem failed with a duplicate-key error
Nothing: DynamoDB undoes a request whose sender stopped waiting
warmup.why: PutItem replaces any item with the same key, without a word, so an identical repeat leaves one item. Only a condition on the write makes the second one fail, and the third section builds that. The third option is the tempting one if you've met PostgreSQL's unique indexes. And if the item's key had contained the time the request arrived, the repeat would have built a new key, and you'd have two items. That's the trap this lesson is about.

sections.h: DynamoDB is a hash map of small sorted maps
sections.body:
Let's start with the simplest store a key can serve. The cloakroom at a theatre is one. You hand over a coat and get ticket 47. Later you hand back ticket 47 and get your coat, in seconds, whether the room holds 50 coats or 5,000. Ask the attendant for "every blue coat", though, and she has to walk past every hook.

A key-value store works the same way. It has two operations, `put(key, value)` and `get(key)`. The key is the ticket and the value is the coat: the store never looks inside it. It hashes the key, turning it into a number that picks a partition, one slice of the data held by a few machines. So both operations cost the same, however big the table grows. Redis, a store that keeps keys and values in memory, is one example, with its own track. Amazon DynamoDB is another. It's a database that Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon's business that rents out computers over the internet, runs for you: you create tables, and AWS runs the machines. Each partition keeps copies in several availability zones, separate data centres in one area that AWS calls a Region. One copy acts as the leader, as Why other data models exist described.

We want two things from a payments store, whether it holds 50 million payments or 5 billion. One is to fetch a payment by its key in a few milliseconds. The other is to list an account's newest payments. A pure key-value store does the first and fails the second. "A-1001's newest payments" isn't one key, and the store can't see inside its values, so it would have to read everything. Two database researchers, Stonebraker and Pavlo, made the same point about the whole family. Once a value has several fields, your code must unpack it, and every other way of finding things is code you write.

So DynamoDB grew into a store of records with named fields. It calls each record an item. Here's one, the way DynamoDB's interface sends it:

```json
{
  "pk":          { "S": "ACCT#A-1001" },
  "sk":          { "S": "PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:03.120Z#pay-81723" },
  "amountMinor": { "N": "4250" },
  "currency":    { "S": "EUR" }
}
```

Each attribute, DynamoDB's word for a field, has a name and a typed value. `S` marks a string and `N` a number, sent as text so no digits are lost; there are also binary data, lists, maps and sets. An item can be at most 400 KB. When you create a table, you declare only the key; every other attribute is up to each item.

This table's key has two attributes, the two-part address from the last lesson. `pk` is the partition key: DynamoDB hashes it to pick the partition, so it only ever answers "equals". `sk` is the sort key: DynamoDB stores all items with the same `pk` together, sorted by `sk`. That sorted group is an item collection. In the cloakroom, it's one rail per family, with each family's coats hung in order. **The picture for this lesson is a hash map from partition key to a small sorted map.** It's the last two lessons' ideas in one table: hash to place the data, sort to make ranges cheap. The `ACCT#` and `PAY#` prefixes let different kinds of item share one collection, which the next lesson builds on.

Reads are eventually consistent by default: any copy may answer, including one that hasn't yet received a write that finished a moment ago. Set `ConsistentRead` to true and the leader answers, so you see every write that has finished. That's a strongly consistent read, and it costs twice as much. Global secondary indexes, the second copies from the last lesson, can't do strongly consistent reads at all.

DynamoDB charges by item size, so sizes matter. A read unit covers one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent ones. A write unit covers one write per second of up to 1 KB. So a 300-byte payment costs one write unit to write, and half a read unit to read. Each partition tops out at 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units a second. A partition key that everyone writes to, like one huge shop on the year's busiest shopping day, hits that ceiling whatever the table's settings say. Big items hit it sooner: a 400 KB item costs 400 write units, so one partition takes about 2.5 such writes a second. Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys, in the Partitioning track, spreads that load.

The cloakroom breaks in one place: a real one has a fixed number of hooks, while DynamoDB splits a partition that grows or gets busy, without asking you. Next, we'll stop building items as maps by hand.

aside.title: Can I run DynamoDB on my own computer?
aside.body: Not the real one: DynamoDB runs only in AWS's data centres, and you pay for what you use. For learning and testing, AWS gives away DynamoDB Local, a small program that answers the same requests on your laptop. This lesson's Try-its and lab use it. It's for development only: it doesn't split tables into partitions, it ignores the capacity settings a real table has, and it runs on your one machine.

try.title: Look inside an item collection
steps: From the `labs` folder, start DynamoDB Local 3.3.2 in Docker, a program that runs small separate machines, called containers, on your computer: `docker compose -f env/dynamodb.yml up -d`. It keeps its data in memory, listens on port 8000 and accepts any credentials (the name and secret that prove to AWS who you are). Leave it running for this lesson's other Try-its.

Read `ItemCollectionDemo.kt`. It creates a table, then writes five items in a scrambled order: four for account A-1001 and one for A-2002. Predict the order in which the Query prints A-1001's sort keys.

code.title: ItemCollectionDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
Query pk = ACCT#A-1001:
  META
  PAY#2026-11-06T18:40:51.004Z#pay-80911
  PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:03.120Z#pay-81723
  REFUND#2026-11-07T11:02:00.000Z#ref-12
GetItem (ACCT#A-1001, META): {sk=AttributeValue(S=META), customerId=AttributeValue(S=C-77), currency=AttributeValue(S=EUR), pk=AttributeValue(S=ACCT#A-1001)}
```

DynamoDB returns the item collection in sort-key order, comparing the bytes of the text (UTF-8, the usual way to store text as bytes). `M` comes before `P`, which comes before `R`, so META, then the payments in time order, then the refund. A-2002's item never appears, because a Query reads one item collection. GetItem needs both key attributes, and it prints the raw item: a map of typed `AttributeValue`s. The map's printed order can differ on your machine, because it's a hash map.

sections.h: From a Kotlin class to an item: the Enhanced Client
sections.body:
The item above, built in code, is a `Map<String, AttributeValue>`, with a typed wrapper around every value. That's what `DynamoDbClient` makes you write. It's the low-level client in the AWS SDK for Java 2.x, the library AWS ships so Java and Kotlin programs can call its services. The demo in the last section used it. You'd rather write a Kotlin class and let a library convert it. The Enhanced Client is that library, built on top of the low-level client.

You reach DynamoDB Local with the normal client and an endpoint override, which points the client at your laptop instead of at AWS. Any credentials work locally, but the SDK insists on having some, and on a Region:

```kotlin
val low = DynamoDbClient.builder()
    .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
    .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
    .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
    .build()
val enhanced = DynamoDbEnhancedClient.builder().dynamoDbClient(low).build()
```

The simplest mapping comes from a bean, an old Java convention: a class with a constructor that takes no arguments, plus a getter and a setter for each property. A Kotlin data class doesn't have that shape, so use a plain class with `var` properties and default values. The annotations, the `@` markers that tell the library which property is which part of the key, must sit on the getter. That's what the `@get:` prefix does:

```kotlin
@DynamoDbBean
class PaymentItem {
    @get:DynamoDbPartitionKey
    var pk: String = ""

    @get:DynamoDbSortKey
    var sk: String = ""

    var paymentId: String = ""
    var amountMinor: Long = 0     // cents: no Double near money
    var createdAt: String = ""
}

val payments = enhanced.table("payments", TableSchema.fromBean(PaymentItem::class.java))
payments.putItem(item)
val back = payments.getItem(Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-1001").sortValue(item.sk).build())
```

`amountMinor` is in cents, a whole number, because whole numbers add up exactly and a `Double` sometimes doesn't. If you'd rather keep classes that never change once built, the Enhanced Client also supports `@DynamoDbImmutable` classes with a builder, and `StaticTableSchema` for a schema written in code. The lab maps two classes, `PaymentItem` and `IdempotencyItem`, onto one table: the Enhanced Client only needs each class's key attributes to match the table's.

One habit of `putItem` matters for payments. If an item with the same key already exists, PutItem replaces it: no error, no warning, and the old attributes are gone. In the cloakroom, it's an attendant who takes the coat off hook 47 and hangs someone else's there without a word. That was the warm-up's answer. Next, we'll turn it from a problem into a tool.

sections.h: Storing a payment once when it arrives twice: a conditional write
sections.body:
Payment requests arrive more than once, for ordinary reasons. The card reader doesn't hear back in time and sends again, as in the opening. The program crashes after its write landed, restarts and handles the request again. Two copies of the program run at once, for speed, and the same request reaches both. Each repeat carries the same request, and none of them may create a second payment.

An operation that has the same effect however many times it runs is called idempotent. So the card reader marks every request with an idempotency key. It's a value the card reader makes up once for each payment, often a UUID (a random 128-bit id), and sends again with every retry. The store must make sure each key creates at most one payment. Let's build that up.

Version 1 checks, then writes: `GetItem` the key, and if nothing comes back, `PutItem` the payment. Now two workers, two copies of the program, handle the same request 2 ms apart. Both `GetItem` calls run before either `PutItem`, both see nothing, and both create a payment. Checking and then acting in two separate requests is a race, a bug whose result depends on which caller gets there first, whenever two callers can run at once.

Version 2 writes a claim, an item whose key comes from the idempotency key, `pk = IDEMP#9f1c` and `sk = IDEMP`, so both workers write the same item. But a plain `PutItem` replaces an existing item without a word. Both writes succeed, both workers believe they won, and both go on to create a payment.

Version 3 adds a condition expression. **A write can carry a condition, and DynamoDB checks it against the target item and applies the write in one step:**

```kotlin
val unclaimed = Expression.builder()
    .expression("attribute_not_exists(pk) OR expiresAt < :now")
    .putExpressionValue(":now", AttributeValue.fromN(now.toString()))
    .build()
claims.putItem(
    PutItemEnhancedRequest.builder(IdempotencyItem::class.java)
        .item(claim)                       // pk = IDEMP#<key>, sk = IDEMP
        .conditionExpression(unclaimed)
        .build()
)
```

`attribute_not_exists(pk)` is true only when no item with this exact key exists. If the condition is false, DynamoDB writes nothing, throws `ConditionalCheckFailedException`, and still charges the write units. The worker that lost then reads the claim and returns the first payment's id, so every caller gets the same answer. In the cloakroom, it's an attendant who checks the hook and hangs the coat in one movement, so nobody can slip in between. The condition only works if every retry builds the same key. Put the arrival time or a fresh UUID into the claim's key, and each retry writes a new item that the condition never sees.

Version 4 makes claims expire. They can't live forever: at 2,000 new payments a second, one day adds about 173 million claims. So each claim stores `expiresAt`, a Number of seconds since 1 January 1970, called Unix time. Then you turn on TTL (time to live) for that attribute, and DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background, typically within a few days of expiry, without charging write units. Until then the expired claim is still in the table, which is why the condition also accepts `expiresAt < :now`.

One gap is left. The claim and the payment are two separate writes. If the program dies between them, a retry finds the claim and reports a payment that was never written. DynamoDB single-table design and transactions, the next lesson, closes that gap with `TransactWriteItems`, DynamoDB's call for writing several items all or nothing.

frames.say: Worker 2 reads the claim with a strongly consistent read. The claim's fingerprint, a short summary of the request (account, shop, amount and currency), matches its own request, so it returns `Replayed(pay-81723)` without writing anything. Worker 1 goes on to write the payment item and returns `Created(pay-81723)`. Both callers give the same answer.

code.title: ConditionalPutDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.model.l03.demo

import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.StaticCredentialsProvider
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.DynamoDbEnhancedClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.Expression
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.Key
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.TableSchema
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.mapper.annotations.DynamoDbBean
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.mapper.annotations.DynamoDbPartitionKey
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.mapper.annotations.DynamoDbSortKey
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.model.PutItemEnhancedRequest
import software.amazon.awssdk.enhanced.dynamodb.model.QueryConditional
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.DynamoDbClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ConditionalCheckFailedException
import java.net.URI

/** A Kotlin class the Enhanced Client can map: var properties with defaults, key annotations on the getters. */
@DynamoDbBean
class DemoPayment {
    @get:DynamoDbPartitionKey
    var pk: String = ""

    @get:DynamoDbSortKey
    var sk: String = ""

    var amountMinor: Long = 0
}

/** Three ways to write "the same" payment twice. Only one of them notices. */
fun main() {
    val low = DynamoDbClient.builder()
        .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
        .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
        .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
        .build()
    val enhanced = DynamoDbEnhancedClient.builder().dynamoDbClient(low).build()
    val table = enhanced.table("demo-conditional", TableSchema.fromBean(DemoPayment::class.java))
    runCatching { table.deleteTable() } // start clean on every run
    table.createTable()

    fun payment(pk: String, sk: String, amount: Long) =
        DemoPayment().apply { this.pk = pk; this.sk = sk; amountMinor = amount }
    val key = Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-1001").sortValue("PAY#pay-81723").build()

    // 1. plain PutItem twice with the same key: the second silently replaces the first
    table.putItem(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-81723", 4250))
    table.putItem(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-81723", 9900))
    println("1. plain put twice: no error, amountMinor is now ${table.getItem(key).amountMinor}")

    // 2. the same write with a condition: only if no item with this key exists yet
    val mustBeNew = Expression.builder().expression("attribute_not_exists(pk)").build()
    fun putIfNew(item: DemoPayment) = table.putItem(
        PutItemEnhancedRequest.builder(DemoPayment::class.java).item(item).conditionExpression(mustBeNew).build()
    )
    putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-90001", 4250))
    println("2. conditional put of pay-90001: written")
    try {
        putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-1001", "PAY#pay-90001", 4250))
    } catch (e: ConditionalCheckFailedException) {
        println("   again: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.awsErrorDetails().errorMessage()}")
    }

    // 3. the trap: the sort key contains the ARRIVAL time, and the retry arrives 3 seconds later
    putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-2002", "PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:03.120Z", 4250))
    putIfNew(payment("ACCT#A-2002", "PAY#2026-11-07T10:15:06.480Z", 4250))
    val copies = table.query(QueryConditional.keyEqualTo(Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-2002").build()))
        .items().count()
    println("3. retry with a time-based key: both conditional puts succeeded, A-2002 now has $copies payments")
    low.close()
}

try.expect:
```text
1. plain put twice: no error, amountMinor is now 9900
2. conditional put of pay-90001: written
   again: ConditionalCheckFailedException: The conditional request failed
3. retry with a time-based key: both conditional puts succeeded, A-2002 now has 2 payments
```

Case 1 is the silent overwrite: the second put wins, and nobody is told. Case 2 is the fix: same key, so the second write is refused. Case 3 is the trap. The condition worked exactly as written, but the retry built a different key, so there was nothing for it to find, and the account now shows the payment twice.

sections.h: Reading an account's newest payments: Query, not Scan
sections.body:
`GetItem` needs the whole key, both `pk` and `sk`. For "A-1001's 20 newest payments" you know the partition key, but none of the sort keys. `Scan` would read every item in the table. `Query` is the read made for an item collection.

A Query must give the partition key with `=`. It may add one condition on the sort key: `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `BETWEEN` or `begins_with`. DynamoDB goes to the partition, finds the first matching item in sort order and reads forward, or backward when you set `ScanIndexForward` to false. AP1 from the last lesson, an account's payments newest first, is one Query:

```kotlin
val onlyPayments = QueryConditional.sortBeginsWith(
    Key.builder().partitionValue("ACCT#A-1001").sortValue("PAY#").build()
)
val newest = payments.query(
    QueryEnhancedRequest.builder()
        .queryConditional(onlyPayments)
        .scanIndexForward(false)   // newest first
        .limit(20)                 // DynamoDB stops after 20 items
        .build()
).items().take(20)                 // and Kotlin stops asking for pages
```

`begins_with(sk, "PAY#")` keeps the read to payments: `META` sorts before them and refunds sort after them. Reading backward starts at the newest. In the cloakroom, it's walking to one family's rail, starting at the end where the newest coats hang, and taking 20.

Results come in pages. One Query call returns at most 1 MB, counted before any filter. If there's more, the answer carries `LastEvaluatedKey`, the key where it stopped, and the next call starts from there. The Enhanced Client's `items()` follows the pages for you, fetching each one only when you ask for more.

Two other tools look similar and cost far more. A `FilterExpression` runs after the read, so a Query with a filter pays for every item in its run and returns only some of them. A `Scan` reads the whole table, page by page. Keep Scan for exports and one-off repairs of old data, and never run one each time a customer asks for something.

String sort keys sort by their UTF-8 bytes, so a time inside a key must have a fixed width and one time zone. `Instant.toString()`, the usual way to print a moment in time on the JVM, drops zero milliseconds. That makes `10:15:03Z` sort after `10:15:03.120Z`, because `Z` comes after `.` in byte order. The lab formats every time as `yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'` for that reason.

That's the limit of an item collection: it answers questions about one partition key. A question by shop needs a second copy of the data under another key. And a screen that wants the account's own item and its newest payments in one Query needs sort keys named with care, since `META` sorts before every payment. The next lesson builds both.

code.title: QueryCostDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.model.l03.demo

import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials
import software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.StaticCredentialsProvider
import software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.DynamoDbClient
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.AttributeDefinition
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.AttributeValue
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.BillingMode
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.KeySchemaElement
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.KeyType
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.PutRequest
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ReturnConsumedCapacity
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.ScalarAttributeType
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.dynamodb.model.WriteRequest
import java.net.URI
import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneOffset
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter

/** 2,000 payments for 100 accounts. Three ways to find one account's payments, and what each one reads. */
fun main() {
    val ddb = DynamoDbClient.builder()
        .endpointOverride(URI.create("http://localhost:8000"))
        .region(Region.US_EAST_1)
        .credentialsProvider(StaticCredentialsProvider.create(AwsBasicCredentials.create("sfz", "sfz")))
        .build()
    val table = "demo-query-cost"
    runCatching { ddb.deleteTable { it.tableName(table) } }
    ddb.createTable {
        it.tableName(table)
            .attributeDefinitions(
                AttributeDefinition.builder().attributeName("pk").attributeType(ScalarAttributeType.S).build(),
                AttributeDefinition.builder().attributeName("sk").attributeType(ScalarAttributeType.S).build(),
            )
            .keySchema(
                KeySchemaElement.builder().attributeName("pk").keyType(KeyType.HASH).build(),
                KeySchemaElement.builder().attributeName("sk").keyType(KeyType.RANGE).build(),
            )
            .billingMode(BillingMode.PAY_PER_REQUEST)
    }

    // seed: account A-0000 .. A-0099, 20 payments each, amounts 500..10,000 cents
    val fmt = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'").withZone(ZoneOffset.UTC)
    val start = Instant.parse("2026-11-01T00:00:00Z")
    val items = (0 until 2_000).map { i ->
        val account = "A-%04d".format(i % 100)
        val at = fmt.format(start.plusSeconds(i * 157L))
        mapOf(
            "pk" to s("ACCT#$account"), "sk" to s("PAY#$at#pay-$i"),
            "accountId" to s(account), "amountMinor" to n(500L + (i * 7919L) % 9_501),
        )
    }
    items.chunked(25).forEach { batch -> // BatchWriteItem takes at most 25 items
        ddb.batchWriteItem { it.requestItems(mapOf(table to batch.map { item ->
            WriteRequest.builder().putRequest(PutRequest.builder().item(item).build()).build()
        })) }
    }

    // A. Query: one partition, one range, read from the end
    val a = ddb.query {
        it.tableName(table)
            .keyConditionExpression("pk = :pk AND begins_with(sk, :pay)")
            .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":pk" to s("ACCT#A-0042"), ":pay" to s("PAY#")))
            .scanIndexForward(false).limit(5)
            .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
    }
    println("A. Query, newest 5:          returned %4d, read %4d, capacity units %s".format(a.count(), a.scannedCount(), a.consumedCapacity()?.capacityUnits()))
    a.items().take(2).forEach { println("     ${it["sk"]!!.s()}") }

    // B. Query plus a filter: the filter runs AFTER the read
    val b = ddb.query {
        it.tableName(table)
            .keyConditionExpression("pk = :pk")
            .filterExpression("amountMinor > :big")
            .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":pk" to s("ACCT#A-0042"), ":big" to n(8_000)))
            .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
    }
    println("B. Query + filter > 80.00:   returned %4d, read %4d, capacity units %s".format(b.count(), b.scannedCount(), b.consumedCapacity()?.capacityUnits()))

    // C. Scan with a filter on a non-key attribute: reads the whole table to find 20 items
    val c = ddb.scanPaginator {
        it.tableName(table)
            .filterExpression("accountId = :acct")
            .expressionAttributeValues(mapOf(":acct" to s("A-0042")))
            .returnConsumedCapacity(ReturnConsumedCapacity.TOTAL)
    }.toList()
    println("C. Scan + filter on account: returned %4d, read %4d, capacity units %s".format(
        c.sumOf { it.count() }, c.sumOf { it.scannedCount() }, c.sumOf { it.consumedCapacity()?.capacityUnits() ?: 0.0 }))
    ddb.close()
}

private fun s(v: String): AttributeValue = AttributeValue.fromS(v)
private fun n(v: Long): AttributeValue = AttributeValue.fromN(v.toString())

try.expect:
```text
A. Query, newest 5:          returned    5, read    5, capacity units 0.5
     PAY#2026-11-04T12:41:34.000Z#pay-1942
     PAY#2026-11-04T08:19:54.000Z#pay-1842
B. Query + filter > 80.00:   returned    4, read   20, capacity units 0.5
C. Scan + filter on account: returned   20, read 2000, capacity units 20.0
```

`read` is DynamoDB's `ScannedCount` and `returned` is its `Count`. The Query reads exactly what it returns, newest first. The filter in B reads all 20 of the account's items to return 4, so it costs the same as reading all 20. The Scan reads all 2,000 items to return 20, and costs 40 times as much as the Query. At 50 million payments, it would read 50 million.

compare.note: Both send the same PutItem request with the same condition. The Enhanced Client turns your object into attributes; it doesn't hide the interface underneath, so conditions, keys and pages work the same way. The raw client is handy in tools and tests, where you want to see exactly what's stored. The Enhanced Client keeps the program's own code typed. Either way, `ConditionalCheckFailedException` is the signal that someone else's item is already there.

worked.title: Trace a retried payment through createPayment

steps.say: A request arrives at 10:00:00 UTC with idempotency key `9f1c` and payment id `pay-81723`. `createPayment` builds the claim. Its key comes only from the idempotency key; the time goes into `expiresAt`. The fingerprint is a short summary of the request, used later to tell a true repeat from a different request that reuses the key.
steps.code:
val now = cmd.at.epochSecond                       // 1794045600
val claim = IdempotencyItem().apply {
    pk = claimKey(cmd.idempotencyKey)             // IDEMP#9f1c
    sk = CLAIM_SORT_KEY                           // IDEMP
    paymentId = cmd.paymentId                     // pay-81723
    fingerprint = cmd.fingerprint()               // A-1001|M-0042|4250|EUR
    expiresAt = now + CLAIM_TTL_SECONDS           // 1794132000
}

steps.say: The conditional put succeeds, so the program writes the payment item next. The table now holds two items in two partitions.

pk            sk                                       attributes
IDEMP#9f1c    IDEMP                                    paymentId=pay-81723, expiresAt=1794132000
ACCT#A-1001   PAY#2026-11-07T10:00:00.000Z#pay-81723   amountMinor=4250, status=AUTHORIZED

steps.say: The card reader didn't hear back in time, so it retries 3 seconds later with the same key and the same request. The claim's key is identical, the condition finds the live item, and DynamoDB throws. The catch block reads the claim with a strongly consistent read and compares fingerprints.

Two more cases, both covered by the lab's tests. The same key with a different amount is a `Mismatch`: the program should refuse it, not hand back the old payment. And 25 hours later the claim has expired. TTL may not have deleted it yet, but `expiresAt < :now` is true, so the key can be used again.
steps.code:
retry, same body, 3 s later    -> Replayed(pay-81723)   nothing written
same key, amount 9900          -> Mismatch(pay-81723)   nothing written
same key, 25 hours later       -> Created(pay-2)        claim replaced

lab.title: Store payments in DynamoDB Local, once per idempotency key
steps: Docker must be running. The tests start DynamoDB Local 3.3.2 through Testcontainers, a library that starts a container for each test run (the first run downloads it), and give every test its own table. You don't need the DynamoDB Local you started for the Try-its.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All seven fail with `NotImplementedError` for now.
Read `PaymentItems.kt`. It holds the two item classes that share one table, the request, and the three possible results. Nothing to change there.
Write `recentPayments` in `PaymentStore.kt` as one Query: `begins_with` on `PAY#`, `scanIndexForward(false)`, and a limit. Two tests pass.
Write `createPayment`: the conditional put of the claim, then the payment, then the catch block that reads the claim and compares fingerprints. All seven pass.
Run the tests three more times. The test for workers running at once fires eight identical requests together, and it must pass every time.
hints: `payments.query(request).items()` is an `Iterable` that fetches pages only as you walk it, so `.take(limit)` returns a `List` and stops asking for pages.
Values in an expression are typed: `.putExpressionValue(":now", AttributeValue.fromN(now.toString()))`. Numbers travel as strings.
A strongly consistent read with the Enhanced Client: `claims.getItem { r -> r.key(key); r.consistentRead(true) }`.
If the retry test finds two payment items, your claim's key isn't built from the idempotency key alone.

drill.title: The claim's conditional put from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. Write the Kotlin that puts an `IdempotencyItem` named `claim` into the table `claims`, only if no live claim exists (none at all, or one whose `expiresAt` is before `now`). Return `true` if this caller won and `false` if someone else holds the key.

recap: A key-value store answers "the value for this key" at the same cost at any size, and nothing else. DynamoDB adds a sort key: items with the same partition key form an item collection, stored together and sorted.

DynamoDB charges by item size: a read unit covers 4 KB, a write unit 1 KB, and one partition tops out at 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second. Default reads may be a moment behind; `ConsistentRead` asks the leader.
PutItem silently replaces an item with the same key. A condition such as `attribute_not_exists(pk)` makes the check and the write one step on that item.
An idempotency claim's key must come from the idempotency key alone. TTL deletes expired items lazily, so the condition must also accept an expired claim.
Query reads one item collection, optionally one sort-key range, forward or backward, up to 1 MB per page. Filters run after the read, and Scan reads the whole table.
The limit: the claim and the payment are two writes, so a crash between them leaves a claim with no payment. And one item collection answers only questions about one partition key.
closing:
We started with a card reader that sent one payment twice. A plain PutItem stored it once by luck, and would have stored it twice if the key held the arrival time. A conditional write on a key built from the idempotency key stores it once every time, and tells the second sender who won.

Look at the confirmation page of your next online order. Many show a long reference code. Ask yourself whether pressing Pay again would send the same code, or a new one.

Next, we'll fit an account, its payments and its refunds into one table, and move money between two accounts with writes that happen together or not at all.

quiz.q: A table has the key attributes `pk` and `sk`. You `PutItem` the key (`ACCT#A-1001`, `PAY#...#pay-81723`) with the condition `attribute_not_exists(pk)`. An item with the same `pk` but a different `sk` already exists. What happens?
options: The write succeeds: the condition looks only at the item with this exact pk and sk
The write fails, because `pk` already exists in the partition
The write fails with an error, because `pk` always exists
The write succeeds and replaces the other item in the partition
quiz.why: DynamoDB checks a condition against the one item named by the request's full key. No item has this pk and sk, so `attribute_not_exists(pk)` is true. The second option is the tempting one: other items in the same collection share the pk, but the condition never looks at them, and a put never touches an item with a different key.

quiz.q: An account has 20 payments. A Query on its partition with the filter `amountMinor > 8000` returns 4 items. What did it read?
options: 4 items, because the filter runs inside the index
Every item in the table
All 20 of the account's items; the filter dropped 16 after reading them
Nothing until the filter matched, then 4 items
quiz.why: A filter runs after the Query reads its slice, so you pay for all 20 items and get 4. That's why `ScannedCount` and `Count` differ. It isn't a read of the whole table, though: the key condition still keeps the read to one item collection.

quiz.q: A claim's `expiresAt` passed two hours ago, and TTL is on for that attribute. What does a GetItem for the claim return now?
options: Nothing: TTL deletes an item the moment it expires
Possibly the item: TTL deletes typically within a few days, so check `expiresAt` yourself
An error saying the item has expired
The item, but with every attribute except the key removed
quiz.why: TTL deletion is work done in the background, typically within a few days of expiry. Until then the item is an ordinary item. That's why the lab's condition treats `expiresAt < :now` as free, and why AWS suggests leaving expired items out of reads yourself.

quiz.q: Which of these reads can be strongly consistent?
options: A Query on a global secondary index with `ConsistentRead` true
A GetItem on the table with `ConsistentRead` true
Any read on a table you pay for per request
A read from DynamoDB Streams, the feed of changes a table can publish
quiz.why: The table itself, and its local secondary indexes, support strongly consistent reads, answered by the leader. Global secondary indexes and streams are updated a moment after the table, so their reads may always be a moment behind. The first option is the trap: the setting exists on the request, but a global index can't honour it. How you pay for a table doesn't change consistency.

quiz.q: From Model the access patterns first: a payments table has partition key `accountId` and sort key `createdAt`. Support now needs shop M-0042's FAILED payments for any time window, many times an hour. What's the right fix?
options: Scan the table with a filter on merchantId and status
Query every account's partition and filter by shop
Add `createdAt` to the partition key
Add a global secondary index keyed by merchantId, with status then createdAt in the sort key
quiz.why: A new access pattern that runs often needs a key that answers it. With the shop as partition key and status before time in the sort key, `status = FAILED` fixes the first part of the sort key, and the time window is one slice. A Scan, or a Query for every account, costs in proportion to the table. Changing the table's partition key would break AP1.

flashcards.front: What does DynamoDB's PutItem do when an item with the same key exists?
flashcards.back: Replaces it, silently. Add a condition expression if you want the second write refused.

flashcards.front: What does `attribute_not_exists(pk)` check in a PutItem?
flashcards.back: Whether the one item named by this request's full key exists. Not the rest of the item collection.

flashcards.front: What happens when a condition expression is false?
flashcards.back: Nothing is written, DynamoDB throws `ConditionalCheckFailedException`, and the write units are still charged.

flashcards.front: TTL: what format, and how fast?
flashcards.back: A Number attribute holding Unix time in seconds. Expired items are deleted in the background, typically within a few days, at no write cost.

flashcards.front: What do one read unit and one write unit cover?
flashcards.back: Read: one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent ones. Write: one write per second of up to 1 KB.

flashcards.front: How much does one Query call return at most?
flashcards.back: 1 MB, measured before any filter. `LastEvaluatedKey` in the answer means there are more pages.

flashcards.front: How do you write an Enhanced Client bean in Kotlin?
flashcards.back: `@DynamoDbBean` on a class with `var` properties and default values, and the key annotations on the getters: `@get:DynamoDbPartitionKey`, `@get:DynamoDbSortKey`.

terms.plain: One record in a DynamoDB table: a set of named, typed attributes, at most 400 KB.
All items with the same partition key, stored together and sorted by sort key.
A test DynamoDB checks against the target item in the same step as the write. If it's false, nothing is written.
A value the sender attaches to a request, and repeats on every retry, so the store can recognise a repeat and do nothing new.
A Number attribute of Unix time in seconds, after which DynamoDB deletes the item in the background.
How DynamoDB charges: a read unit covers 4 KB read strongly consistently, a write unit covers 1 KB written.
The part of the AWS SDK for Java 2.x that turns your classes into DynamoDB items and back.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a friend why `if (table.getItem(key) == null) table.putItem(item)` doesn't stop a payment from being stored twice in DynamoDB, and what does.
explain_back.answer: It checks, then acts, in two separate requests. Two workers handling the same repeated request can both run the GetItem before either runs the PutItem, so both see nothing and both write. And a plain PutItem never complains about an existing item, it replaces it, so nothing stops the second writer. What works is putting the check inside the write: a PutItem with a condition such as `attribute_not_exists(pk)`. DynamoDB checks the condition and applies the write as one step on that item, so exactly one caller wins and the others get `ConditionalCheckFailedException`. The losers then read the winning claim and return its payment id. Two more things matter. The claim's key must be built from the idempotency key alone, so every retry targets the same item. And an expired claim must count as free, because TTL deletes lazily.
